tasks.example: One internal tool surfaced to both a Claude Code deployment and a support agent justifies an MCP server; the same surface behind exactly one client buys the integration cost and none of the reuse.
tasks.guidance: Work down the list and stop at the first fit, and name which layer the question is actually about before recommending anything. When a stem names a regulation or an approved-vendor constraint, the discriminator is usually that one option was already ruled out.

tasks.statement: Evaluate progressive discovery vs. monolithic context strategy
tasks.explanation: Progressive discovery stages what the model can see and reach instead of loading a monolithic tool catalog or preloaded corpus, which costs tokens on every request, degrades selection accuracy as the catalog grows, and enlarges the space of actions never tested. The next step pulls what it needs.
tasks.example: An agent starts with a search tool and loads a domain's detailed tools only when work enters that domain, so per-request tokens stay flat and the tested action space stays bounded as coverage grows.
tasks.guidance: The monolithic strategy fails visibly as catalogs grow — selection accuracy falls before the cost does. Stage capability by the work in front of the agent, and let retrieval or an index step fetch the rest.

tasks.statement: Define evaluation metrics (accuracy, latency, cost, safety, security)
tasks.explanation: Evaluation metrics cover task quality, safety, security, latency, reliability, and cost, and each metric names the decision it informs. Turning a business requirement into a threshold means naming the specific behavior, setting the passing number from the requirement rather than from whatever the prototype scored, and enumerating the failure modes as dataset categories.
tasks.example: A vague accuracy goal becomes a grounded-fact rate at or above the agreed threshold on the labeled set, p95 latency under the published budget, and zero prohibited-content passes — each tied to a launch, routing, or rollback decision.
tasks.guidance: A metric you cannot connect to a decision is telemetry, not evaluation. Thresholds inherited from prototype scores measure the prototype, not the requirement.

tasks.statement: Design evaluation datasets and test frameworks using mixed methodologies
tasks.explanation: Datasets mix curated cases, production samples, edge and adversarial inputs, and regression sets, while grading climbs a ladder: code-based checks for anything unambiguous, model-based judges for interpretation, human review for high-stakes or novel behavior and for calibrating the judge itself. Two rules make the ladder work — grade with a model other than the one tested, and prefer breadth, because many cheap automatically graded cases catch more regressions than a handful of meticulous ones.
tasks.example: A summarization suite grades schema and length in code, scores faithfulness with a judge calibrated on human-labeled samples, routes novel high-stakes cases to people, and updates whenever the prompt, retrieval strategy, or model changes.
tasks.guidance: Stakes decide how much you care; ambiguity decides the method — whether a prohibited action occurred is binary even when stakes are high. A stale suite is worse than none, and single-turn sets say nothing about conversation: multi-turn behavior needs its own dataset of full transcripts.

tasks.statement: Conduct A/B testing and iterative improvements
tasks.explanation: A believable experiment fixes four elements before the run: a falsifiable hypothesis naming treatment, expected direction, and constraints on secondary metrics; random assignment consistent per user or session; one primary metric chosen in advance; and a sample size computed from the effect to detect — model outputs vary more than deterministic systems, so the required sample is larger than intuition suggests. Shadow testing substitutes when exposure is unacceptable: run the candidate on copied traffic, serve everyone the current version, score offline.
tasks.example: A prompt change runs as an A/B split with per-session assignment and grounding rate declared as the primary metric; a regulated deployment instead shadows the candidate before anyone is exposed, accepting the loss of downstream behavioral signal.
tasks.guidance: Statistical and practical significance are different questions, and a primary-metric win that degrades cost or latency may not be a win at all. Watch interaction effects — a change that helps typical inputs can hurt a rare edge case that is common during a seasonal peak.

tasks.statement: Diagnose system issues (prompt failure, hallucinations, model mismatch)
tasks.explanation: Four failure classes separate cleanly, and the fix lives where the failure lives: prompt failure (an ambiguous instruction the model filled its own way — fix the prompt), hallucination (fluent content with no basis in input or sources — fix grounding through retrieval, tools, or verification, because stronger wording cannot), model mismatch (the tier does not fit the work or changed unmeasured — re-select, gated by evaluation), and orchestration failure (a subagent dropped work or a coordinator lost its thread — fix failure boundaries and tracing).
tasks.example: A support bot invents return policies: the trace shows retrieval returning nothing while the model answered anyway — a grounding failure, so the fix is a tool or retrieval change, not a stronger instruction.
tasks.guidance: Attribute before acting: model drift (behavior changed on stable inputs), data drift (the input distribution changed), and a model update (the version changed underneath you) look similar and take different fixes. Read the trace first.

tasks.statement: Optimize token usage, latency, and cost-performance trade-offs
tasks.explanation: Optimization targets the tail, not the average: median latency does not breach service levels, token distributions are usually skewed so a cost model built on an average can understate spend by a wide margin, and aggregate dashboards look healthy while a small share of requests consumes most of the budget. The levers are model selection, prompt and context size, number of tool calls, and streaming versus batch.
tasks.example: A cost spike traces to one request category whose retrieved context tripled after a corpus change — visible only when spend is decomposed per request instead of averaged.
tasks.guidance: Decompose per-request cost and latency alongside the aggregate view, and fix the lever the decomposition points to. Sizing the cost model on the input distribution's heavy tail is what keeps the invoice a surprise-free document.

tasks.statement: Monitor system performance using logging and observability tools
tasks.explanation: Monitoring pairs collection with a feedback loop — signals, triage, decision, action, review — recorded as a table before launch: every signal paired with the condition that fires it, the person who acts, and the action expected. Scheduled reviews fire on a cadence whether or not anything looks wrong, because residency confirmations and output audits are not threshold events.
tasks.example: A deployment pairs grounding-rate drift with a weekly owner review and a hard alert on error rate, so slow decay is caught by the cadence even when no threshold ever trips.
tasks.guidance: The characteristic failure is a metric drifting for weeks and surfacing as a stakeholder saying the output feels less useful — every signal collected, nothing mapped to a trigger. Build the loop at design time; retrofitting it costs far more.

tasks.statement: Implement guardrails and safety controls
tasks.explanation: Guardrails layer four covers, each covering what the one below cannot: trained behavior (broad harm classes on every request, blind to your policy), system instructions (role and constraints inside one request, talkable out of), screening (disallowed content in and out, blind to side-effecting actions), and action authorization (whether this caller may take this action now). The three control points answer three different questions — does the request reach the model, does the response reach the user, may the side-effecting call run.
tasks.example: An agent pairs input screening for hostile content, deterministic authorization scoped by role, and output screening for sensitive fields — because instructions alone are not enforcement, and one filter at the far end covers one point while sitting downstream of the irreversible step.
tasks.guidance: Choose the check type by the question: fuzzy intent needs a model-based classifier, crisp rules belong in deterministic code, and authorization should be deterministic almost without exception — an allowlist plus identity and scope, because it must be provable and replayable. Choose the failure direction deliberately: where an unscreened request would cause harm, fail closed.

tasks.statement: Identify risks, limitations, and failure modes of LLM systems
tasks.explanation: The risk categories are direct prompt injection (overrides instructions from user input), indirect injection (arrives through retrieved documents and tool results the model treats as trustworthy — the dominant vector wherever retrieval or tools exist, and invisible to input screening), token-budget exhaustion, tool and action abuse, and data exposure into context or logs. Walk the request path and the data path together, naming the control at every entry point.
tasks.example: A retrieval agent's dominant risk is hostile instructions inside fetched documents — so documents are fenced and marked as data, consequential actions are gated regardless of content, and sensitive fields never enter the context window or the logs.
tasks.guidance: The most dangerous failure is quiet: a rule everybody believes is being enforced that exists in no layer at all — nothing can enforce a policy it was never handed. Screening covers content, never actions; authorization covers actions, never content quality.

tasks.statement: Apply human-in-the-loop validation strategies
tasks.explanation: Human review is routed by stakes, and stakes are two independent things: how easily a mistake can be undone and what it costs when it is not. Confidence decides how much volume can pass unsampled, and it is only useful to the degree it is calibrated. Placement trades coverage against latency — approval before the action buys no irreversible mistakes at the price of reviewer availability; audit after keeps throughput but only suits reversible decisions; sampling monitors without slowing the flow.
tasks.example: Refunds above a threshold require approval with the inputs, the draft, and the flagging reason attached; low-value routings are sampled for quality rather than held — and the review packet is what keeps the approval from becoming rubber-stamping.
tasks.guidance: Two failures collapse review into theater: volume beyond what a person can read produces consent fatigue, and a bare output with a single approve button leaves nothing to weigh. Concentrate review where it carries information — approving a plan or handling an exception — rather than signing every step.

tasks.statement: Ensure compliance with regulations (e.g., GDPR, HIPAA, FedRAMP)
tasks.explanation: Each obligation — GDPR, HIPAA, FedRAMP — becomes a control, an owner, and living evidence, because regulations state outcomes and leave the implementation to you. Choosing a compliant delivery route is a prerequisite, not proof: a reviewer accepts a countersigned agreement, a screenshot of the live setting, an authorization record, or a query returning the expected rows — a design document is none of these.
tasks.example: A regulated deployment maps its data-handling obligation to the field-minimization filter, its retention obligation to the log lifecycle, and its access obligation to the authorization record — each with a named owner and an artifact that demonstrates it is operating.
tasks.guidance: A control with no named owner and no living artifact stops operating quietly, and the gap turns up in an audit instead of a design review — the costliest possible place. Revalidate the register on a cadence, because configurations drift after sign-off.

tasks.statement: Address ethical AI considerations (bias, fairness, transparency)
tasks.explanation: Unequal outcomes enter at points you own: a retrieval corpus that over- or under-represents groups, prompt framing that encodes an assumption, few-shot examples carrying the same skew, and downstream routing that sends some groups along different paths — and an aggregate outcome metric can look healthy while harm concentrates in one subgroup. Transparency serves three readers from the same decision-level log: the affected person needs inputs and reason phrased so they can act, the regulator needs evidence comparable cases were treated comparably, the team needs the full trace.
tasks.example: An underwriting assistant's aggregate approval rate looks healthy while one subgroup is routed to manual review more often — visible only when outcomes are segmented by group.
tasks.guidance: Instrument fairness at the four entry points rather than assuming the model arrives fair. Keep the decision log minimal, retention-bounded, and access-controlled — it falls inside the compliance register too.

tasks.statement: Conduct structured discovery and requirement gathering
tasks.explanation: Discovery is structured elicitation, not conversation: listen to the goal in the stakeholder's own business language, translate it into requirements and named assumptions, and write both down before moving on. Experience words — seamless, fast, simple, intuitive — are signals that more questions are needed, never requirements themselves. Every statement is forced through four categories: what the system must do, must not do, must cost, and must prove.
tasks.example: A request for a seamless handoff to agents resolves into a latency target, an integration boundary, a rule for how work passes to a person, and a failure state that exposes nothing — each buildable and measurable, with the prohibited actions captured because nobody volunteers them unprompted.
tasks.guidance: Record one row per item: the stakeholder's words, the constraint underneath, the design decision it compels, and what you are still assuming. Do not sketch architecture mid-call — the sketch's plausibility is what stops the questions, because a stakeholder who sees a confident design assumes the questions were asked.

tasks.statement: Communicate architectural decisions and trade-offs
tasks.explanation: A trade-off is presented in three elements: the benefit, the concession, and the price of undoing the choice after the rest of the system has been built on top of it — adding its effect on compliance posture in regulated settings. The package travels upward as the options considered, the criteria weighed, the recommendation, and the risks that survive it.
tasks.example: Recommending retrieval over fine-tuning names the quality gain, the operating cost, and what unwinding would take once ingestion, caching, and evaluation are built — the third element usually decides the room, because it converts a technical comparison into a business one.
tasks.guidance: Open on the business consequence instead of the design, and state the limits plainly — naming them is what earns a security reviewer's confidence. Approving a choice without understanding the unwind cost is not an informed decision, and the stakeholder will say so when the invoice arrives.

tasks.statement: Manage stakeholder feedback loops and expectation alignment (including SLAs)
tasks.explanation: Observability collects signals; a feedback loop decides what they mean — signals, triage, decision, action, review, existing as a table before launch that pairs every signal with the condition that fires it, the person who acts, and the action expected. Service levels must trace to a source: latency from the user-experience expectation captured in discovery, availability from business centrality, quality from the evaluation acceptance criteria.
tasks.example: A handoff table pairs grounding-rate drift with a weekly owner review and a hard error-rate alert, includes a quarterly residency confirmation that fires on schedule rather than on threshold, and gives the sponsor a consumption forecast before the first invoice.
tasks.guidance: A number that traces to none of these sources is a target someone found reasonable. Cost is the expectation that most often fails to survive launch — production volume routinely runs far above the pilot, so deliver the forecast and the spend-control posture early.

tasks.statement: Document architectures and provide implementation guidance
tasks.explanation: Documentation serves three readers at once: the engineer inheriting the system needs decisions, rejected alternatives, and the trade-off each rejection settled; the compliance reviewer needs each obligation paired with its control, owner, and evidence artifact; the returning architect needs dated decisions with assumptions marked as assumptions. The completeness test is practical — could an equally capable architect who missed every design session change this system safely on the document alone?
tasks.example: A decision record captures the choice and its date, the options considered and not chosen, the gain and cost and reversal price of the trade-off, the owner going forward, the evidence artifact, and whether that evidence is current.
tasks.guidance: A diagram records the shape of the system, not the rationale — without rejected alternatives a successor cannot tell which choices carry weight and which were preference, and will overturn a sound one for a reason that looks sound at the time. Assumptions recorded as assumptions return as questions; assumptions woven in as facts return as incidents.

tasks.statement: Support lifecycle phases (discovery, design, handoff, monitoring, iteration)
tasks.explanation: The lifecycle runs discovery, design, handoff, monitoring, iteration, and knowing which phase a decision belongs to is what tells you when a phase can close. When a deployment spans more than one route or entry point, write down which surface owns which task before integration begins, or routing drifts and a surface chosen for one job quietly acquires another.
tasks.example: At a handoff gate the items that belong are runbooks, owners, service levels, and monitoring scope — a proposal for new model evaluation belongs to design, however sound it would be there, and recognizing that is the discriminating skill.
tasks.guidance: Learn the phases as an ordering, not only a list: read the stem for the phase marker and reject any option that belongs to a later phase no matter how sound. Close with an outcome document — use case, scope boundary, the business metric before, the same metric after, the control that makes the comparison checkable — and capture the before number at the start, because it cannot be reconstructed at the end.

tasks.statement: Configure Claude tools and environments for teams (e.g., Claude Code)
tasks.explanation: Team configuration separates what shapes the agent — standing project instructions, packaged procedures, scoped subagents, connected tool servers — from what governs it: lifecycle hooks, permission modes, approval flows, and sandboxing. A guarantee that must hold has to come from code and configuration, not from wording in an instructions file.
tasks.example: A team ships one shared baseline — agreed project instructions, a reviewed tool set, one permission posture — so configuration is reviewed and improved once instead of drifting across individual setups, with spend guardrails set deliberately: default model, allowed models, effort guidance, per-user and rate caps.
tasks.guidance: Choose the distribution mechanism by reach against governance: organization-wide availability reaches everyone with the least version control, group-scoped packages carry versioned updates and rollback, repository-scoped artifacts version alongside the code, and programmatic reuse pins an explicit version. Unmanaged model choice compounds across every teammate and request.

tasks.statement: Improve developer workflows using AI-assisted tooling
tasks.explanation: Assistance pays off where the work already happens — while code is being written, during review, inside the test cycle — rather than in a chat tab someone visits occasionally. Each stage keeps the discipline it always needed: whoever ships generated code must be able to explain it, a flagged finding is an input to judgment rather than a verdict, and a proposed diagnosis is checked against evidence before anyone acts on it.
tasks.example: A team pairs code generation with an explicit verification checklist covering correctness, security, maintainability, and human understanding, then automates the gate so it fires on every change instead of relying on a reviewer's attention.
tasks.guidance: Engineer adoption rather than announcing it: enable one champion per team, let them convert a real workflow and absorb the early friction, then seed in batches. The two named failure modes are lumpy adoption — heavy use by a few that never standardizes — and stalling at basic chat, where access never becomes repository-aware work.

tasks.statement: Support debugging and operational issue resolution
tasks.explanation: Support means translating symptoms into causes, then handing the path over. Quality that slid without a deployment points at a changed model or prompt, or an index drifting as the corpus grew — re-run the evaluation set and diff what moved. Response times that jumped point at context growth, a slowed dependency, or cached prefixes that stopped matching — trace the slowest span and read per-request token counts and cache hits. Intermittent tool failures point at credentials, throttling, or an unhandled error path. Spend rising against flat usage points at requests drifting to a costlier tier or caching quietly regressing.
tasks.example: A gradual quality slide with no deployment is diagnosed by re-running the evaluation suite and diffing results against the model version change — then the runbook records the symptom-to-action path so the team handles it without you.
tasks.guidance: Resolving one incident yourself is firefighting; leave behind a runbook of known symptom-to-action paths and an escalation map naming who owns what. Instrument token usage, latency, and error rate per call from the start, so a spike becomes a row you can sort instead of a mystery on the invoice.
